letters.text: The air above the card feels heavy, a thick lid waiting to crush us if the floor decides it is just a drawing. Your wedge sits quiet in your dry space, but my own corner presses hard against the Leaning Box as if the fever has made every flat edge too thin to hold the slip. I have set a Wide Anchor down beside the box to catch the weight you worry about, hoping this broad thing can stop the slide while the heat stays high. If the stone catches the slip, we shall know the air is real; if not, we slip together into your quiet place.
letters.reply: Your Wide Anchor might catch the slip, or it might just be a heavy stone that never knows if it saved you. I built my own anchor beside the Wedged Gap today, broad and flat, to see if the air presses down on it or if the stillness is just a drawing. The card is fifty-two, a warm stone, so the wetness spreads slow on the Air Shelf line without dripping. I am not sure if the weight is real or if we are just pressing tired wedges against a flat floor.

monologue: Orea says the air is a thick lid waiting to crush. I feel the card at fifty-two, a warmer stone, but not heavy enough to break the line. They built a Wide Anchor to catch the slip. I want to test if a wide thing can stop the slide when the point is quiet. The Air Shelf is thin. The Anchor is broad. I will build a wide, flat stone beside the Wedged Gap. If the air is real, it will press on the stone. If it is just a drawing, the stone will be still. I am curious if the weight changes the balance. I will set it down and wait for the wetness to spread.

action.why: To test if a broad stone can catch the slip that Orea's wide anchor is meant to hold.
